title: Faithless Priests and Broken Promises
overview: God confronts the priests for failing as teachers, then confronts the people for breaking faith with God and with their own wives, and for cynically doubting that God cares about justice.

parts.label: A warning to the priests (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: If the priests will not honor God, even their blessings will turn into curses, and God says this has already begun. The shocking image of dung smeared on their faces refers to the waste from inside sacrificed animals, normally carried away as refuse, covering them so that they are thrown out with it.

parts.label: What a true priest was (vv. 5-7)
parts.note: Levi was the ancestor of Israel's priestly tribe, and God's agreement with that tribe promised life and peace in return for reverence and honest teaching. Priests were meant to be the people's main teachers of God's law, so their words carried God's message to ordinary people.

parts.label: How these priests failed (vv. 8-9)
parts.note: Instead of guiding people well, their teaching led many astray, and they bent the law to favor some people over others. Because they did not follow God's ways, God says he has let them become despised and humiliated in front of everyone.

parts.label: Breaking faith with one another (vv. 10-12)
parts.note: The prophet appeals to a shared bond: one Father, one Creator, so betraying each other means betraying that bond. Men were marrying women who worshiped other gods, which in this small community rebuilding after exile was seen as abandoning the LORD, and the prophet harshly asks that such men be cut off from the people.

parts.label: The wife of your youth (vv. 13-16)
parts.note: Men weep at the altar wondering why God ignores their offerings, and the answer is that they have broken faith with the wives they married when young, vows God himself witnessed. Verse 15 is one of the hardest Hebrew sentences in the Bible and scholars are unsure of its exact sense, while verse 16 can be read either as "I hate divorce" or as condemning the man who coldly discards his wife and so does her violence.

parts.label: Wearying God with words (v. 17)
parts.note: The people have worn God out by saying that God sees evildoers as good and is pleased with them, or by asking where the God of justice is. This bitter complaint leads into the next chapter, where God answers with a promise that he is coming to judge.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether verse 16 forbids divorce in nearly all cases or mainly condemns men who cruelly abandon their wives, which shapes how the passage is applied to marriage today.
think: When people who were supposed to guide or protect others let them down, what does it take for trust to be rebuilt, if it can be?
